subChunks.title: Bioinformatics — Sequences, Structures & Databases
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora opened a laptop and typed a command. In seconds, a sequence of 30,000 nucleotides appeared on the screen — the complete SARS-CoV-2 genome, compared against 500 other coronavirus sequences, evolutionary relationships displayed as a branching tree. “This analysis,” she said, “took 45 seconds. In 1985, it would have taken a team of scientists three years to generate the sequences alone, and would have been beyond the computational power available to most universities. Bioinformatics is what happens when biology drowns in data.”

Modern biology generates data at an extraordinary rate. A single Illumina sequencing run produces terabytes. The NCBI GenBank contains over 10 trillion nucleotides from millions of organisms. The Protein Data Bank holds over 200,000 three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold2’s structure predictions have transformed structural biology. Making sense of this data requires computational methods — sequence alignment, database search, phylogenetic reconstruction, structural prediction, and statistical analysis — that form the discipline of bioinformatics.

At SENIOR level, bioinformatics is not just using tools but understanding their algorithms, knowing their assumptions, and critically evaluating their outputs. A BLAST result means nothing without understanding the E-value. A phylogenetic tree means nothing without understanding the model of evolution it assumes.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sequence Alignment

Pairwise alignment: Comparing two sequences to identify regions of similarity. The Needleman-Wunsch algorithm (1970) finds the optimal global alignment (end-to-end) by dynamic programming — building a scoring matrix where each cell reflects the best score achievable to align sequences up to that position, considering match scores, mismatch penalties, and gap penalties. The Smith-Waterman algorithm (1981) performs optimal local alignment — identifying the best-matching subsequences within two longer sequences, useful when homology is restricted to functional domains.

Substitution matrices: Not all amino acid substitutions are equally likely. The BLOSUM matrices (Block Substitution Matrix) are derived from empirical frequencies of amino acid substitutions in conserved blocks across distantly related proteins. BLOSUM62 (derived from proteins sharing ~62% identity) is the default for database searches. PAM matrices model evolution probabilistically. The choice of matrix affects sensitivity and specificity of homology detection.

BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool): The most widely used bioinformatics tool. Rather than computing optimal alignments (computationally expensive), BLAST identifies “words” (typically 3 amino acids or 11 nucleotides) matching between query and database sequences, then extends these “hits” into local alignments scored against a substitution matrix. The E-value (expect value) indicates how many alignments of this score or better would be expected by chance in a database of that size — E < 0.001 is generally accepted as significant, but the threshold depends on context (E = 0.01 may be meaningful for a short peptide query; E = 10⁻⁵⁰ is highly significant). E-values are not probabilities; they are expected numbers of random hits.

Multiple sequence alignment (MSA): Aligning three or more sequences simultaneously — essential for phylogenetic analysis, identifying conserved functional residues, and understanding protein families. Clustal Omega, MUSCLE, and MAFFT are widely used programs using progressive alignment (build alignments pairwise, then merge) or iterative refinement. All MSA algorithms are heuristic (optimal MSA is NP-hard for large alignments); the output should always be inspected and manually adjusted where clearly misaligned.

Genomic Databases and Annotation

Major repositories: NCBI GenBank (nucleotide sequences), UniProt (protein sequences — Swiss-Prot is manually curated; TrEMBL is automatically annotated), Protein Data Bank (PDB — 3D structures), Ensembl (genome annotation for eukaryotes), and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA — raw NGS data). Database quality varies enormously: Swiss-Prot (~570,000 entries, manually reviewed with experimental evidence for function) vs TrEMBL (~250 million entries, computationally predicted — many annotations are inferred from sequence similarity, not experimental evidence).

Genome annotation — identifying genes, their boundaries, exon-intron structure, regulatory elements, and function — is a complex computational challenge. Gene prediction tools (Augustus, SNAP) use machine learning trained on known gene structures. RNA-seq data provides direct evidence of transcription and splicing. The human reference genome (GRCh38) is not a single person’s genome but a mosaic consensus — the T2T Consortium (2022) completed the first truly complete gap-free human genome assembly using long-read sequencing.

Phylogenetics

Phylogenetic trees represent evolutionary relationships inferred from sequence data. Key concepts:

Molecular clock hypothesis: Mutations accumulate at roughly constant rates in certain genes — allowing divergence times to be estimated from sequence differences. Strictly neutral changes (synonymous substitutions, some non-coding regions) accumulate most clock-like; adaptive genes (immune genes, viral surface proteins) evolve too rapidly for clock assumptions. Molecular clocks require calibration against the fossil record or biogeographic events.

Tree reconstruction methods: (i) Distance methods (UPGMA, Neighbour-Joining) — convert alignments to pairwise distances and cluster by similarity; fast, suitable for large datasets; (ii) Maximum parsimony — finds the tree requiring the fewest evolutionary changes; computationally intensive; (iii) Maximum likelihood (ML) — evaluates the probability of the observed sequence data given a phylogenetic tree and substitution model; statistically principled; programs: RAxML, IQ-TREE; (iv) Bayesian inference (MrBayes, BEAST) — uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo to sample the posterior distribution of trees, providing credibility intervals on nodes.

Bootstrap support: A statistical measure of node confidence — datasets are resampled with replacement 100–1000 times and the tree rebuilt; bootstrap value at a node indicates the percentage of resampled trees recovering that grouping. Values ≥70% are generally considered supported; <50% are unreliable. Bootstrap is not a p-value — it assesses stability of the tree topology given the data, not a probability of the tree being correct.

Protein Structure Prediction — AlphaFold2

Predicting 3D protein structure from amino acid sequence was the long-standing “protein folding problem.” AlphaFold2 (DeepMind, 2020) solved it — producing structures with accuracy approaching experimental methods for most protein families. AlphaFold2 uses deep learning trained on the PDB, using both multiple sequence alignments (evolutionary information about which residues co-vary) and structural templates. The plDDT (predicted local distance difference test) score quantifies per-residue confidence: >90 is high confidence; 50–70 is low confidence, typically in intrinsically disordered regions. AlphaFold2 is excellent for structural domains with evolutionary information; it performs less well for novel fold families, protein-protein complexes, and intrinsically disordered regions (which lack stable structure). AlphaFold-Multimer extends to protein complexes.

The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (EMBL-EBI) contains structure predictions for ~200 million proteins from UniProt — essentially the entire known proteome. This has transformed structural biology from a bottleneck (months of crystallography or NMR) to near-instant hypothesis generation.

RNA-seq Analysis

RNA sequencing measures genome-wide gene expression. A typical workflow: (i) quality control (FastQC — check read quality, adapter contamination, GC content); (ii) trimming (Trimmomatic, Cutadapt — remove adapters and low-quality bases); (iii) alignment to reference genome (STAR, HISAT2) or pseudo-alignment (Salmon, kallisto — faster); (iv) quantification (DESeq2, edgeR — normalise for sequencing depth and library size, then test for differential expression using negative binomial models); (v) downstream analysis — gene ontology enrichment, pathway analysis, visualisation (heatmaps, volcano plots). Key statistical issues: multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) is essential — testing ~20,000 genes simultaneously at p<0.05 would yield ~1,000 false positives by chance. Batch effects (samples processed on different days or platforms) are a major source of systematic error, addressed by ComBat or limma-removeBatchEffect.

storyBeats.text: Theodora ran a BLAST search live. “The query is a new bacterial enzyme sequence. The top hit has E = 10⁻⁸⁵ and 43% identity to a known cellulase. What do you conclude?”
“That it’s almost certainly homologous to that cellulase — shares the same ancestor — and probably has similar function? 43% identity and that E-value seems really strong.”

“Almost certainly homologous — yes, the E-value makes chance vanishingly unlikely. But ‘probably similar function’ requires care. Sequence similarity predicts function reasonably well for highly conserved core functions. But evolutionary divergence at 43% identity means active site residues may have shifted, substrate specificity may differ, and regulation may be completely different. Homology tells you history; it does not automatically tell you biochemistry. That requires wet-lab validation.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a BLAST search does — how does it find similar sequences in a database, and what does the E-value tell you? Use an analogy to make the concept of database searching intuitive.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between global and local sequence alignment algorithms (Needleman-Wunsch vs Smith-Waterman) and describe how BLAST achieves fast database searching — including what the E-value means and how to interpret it
Describe the principles of phylogenetic tree construction, including substitution models, bootstrap support, and the molecular clock — and critically evaluate tree topology claims
Explain how RNA-seq data is generated, quality-controlled, and analysed for differential gene expression, including the statistical requirements for multiple testing correction
Critically evaluate AlphaFold2 protein structure predictions — including the plDDT confidence score, what the model does well, and where it should not be trusted without experimental validation
commonMistakes: Treating BLAST E-value as a probability — an E-value of 0.001 means approximately 0.001 random hits of this quality are expected by chance, not that there is a 0.1% probability of a random match

Interpreting sequence homology directly as functional equivalence — homologous proteins share evolutionary ancestry but may have diverged substantially in substrate specificity, regulation, or interaction partners

Accepting phylogenetic trees as ground truth rather than hypotheses — trees reflect the sequence data and model assumptions; different models, outgroups, or data subsets can produce different topologies, especially for poorly resolved nodes

Ignoring batch effects in RNA-seq analysis — samples processed at different times or by different operators often show systematic technical differences that can be misinterpreted as biological differences if not corrected
assessmentCriteria: Can interpret a BLAST output correctly: identify the E-value, percentage identity, query coverage, and what each tells the researcher — and identify situations where a ‘significant’ BLAST hit might not indicate genuine homology

Can describe the key steps in RNA-seq analysis from raw reads to a list of differentially expressed genes, identifying at least three quality control steps and the statistical method for multiple testing correction
Can read a phylogenetic tree: identify clades, the position of an outgroup, the meaning of branch length, and interpret bootstrap support values correctly

Can evaluate an AlphaFold2 structure prediction critically using the plDDT score — identifying regions of high and low confidence and explaining why low-confidence regions should not be used for functional inference
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
You are investigating a novel protein found in a marine bacterium, with potential applications in bioplastic degradation. You submit its 312 amino acid sequence to BLASTP (protein BLAST) against the UniProt database. The results include:

  • Hit 1: E = 2 × 10⁻¹¹², 67% identity, 98% query coverage — ‘PETase, Ideonella sakaiensis’ (experimentally characterised PET-degrading enzyme)
  • Hit 2: E = 5 × 10⁻⁴⁵, 34% identity, 87% query coverage — ‘Cutinase, Thermobifida cellulosilytica’ (experimentally characterised)
  • Hit 3: E = 0.082, 18% identity, 45% query coverage — ‘Serine hydrolase, uncultured bacterium, TPA: reassembled’ (computationally predicted from metagenome)
  1. Rank these hits from most to least informative for predicting your protein’s function. Justify your ranking.
  2. Both Hit 1 and Hit 2 suggest your protein belongs to the serine hydrolase superfamily. What additional information would you use to determine whether it likely degrades PET specifically or has broader ester-hydrolysing activity?
  3. Hit 3 has E = 0.082. Should this be considered a significant hit? What concerns exist with the annotation of this database entry?
  4. You obtain an AlphaFold2 prediction of your protein’s structure with plDDT scores of 95 for the central α/β hydrolase fold domain but 32–45 for a 40-residue C-terminal region. How should you interpret these scores, and what do they suggest about the C-terminal region?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Ranking hits by informativeness:
Most informative: Hit 1 (E = 2×10⁻¹¹², 67% identity, 98% coverage, experimentally characterised PETase). The extremely low E-value indicates homology is almost certainly genuine; 67% identity is well above the ~30% “twilight zone” and strongly suggests shared structure and likely shared function; near-complete query coverage means the full sequence is similar. Being experimentally characterised (not just annotated) provides reliable functional evidence.
Second: Hit 2 (E = 5×10⁻⁴⁵, 34% identity, 87% coverage, experimentally characterised cutinase). Still highly significant E-value; 34% identity is in the “twilight zone” where structure is often conserved but function may differ; near complete coverage; experimentally characterised — reliable annotation.
Least informative: Hit 3 (E = 0.082, 18% identity, 45% coverage, computationally predicted). E-value at this level may represent a random match; 18% identity over only 45% of the query is not convincing homology evidence; “TPA: reassembled” indicates it was computationally assembled from metagenome data with no experimental validation. This hit should not be used to infer function.

2. Additional information for functional specificity:
(i) Active site residues: align your sequence with the PETase and cutinase and check whether the catalytic triad (Ser-His-Asp in serine hydrolases) is conserved; also check for PET-specific substrate-binding residues identified in PETase crystal structures (W185 and Y58 in I. sakaiensis PETase are critical for aromatic substrate binding). (ii) Structural comparison: compare AlphaFold2 structure with PETase crystal structure (PDB: 6ANE) — is the active site geometry conserved? Does the binding cleft have the same dimensions and hydrophobic character? (iii) Substrate docking: in silico docking of PET monomer fragments into the predicted structure can suggest binding preference. (iv) Phylogenetic analysis: place your protein in a phylogeny with characterised serine hydrolases to determine whether it falls within the PETase clade or a broader cutinase clade. (v) Wet-lab validation: enzyme assays with BHET (bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate) as substrate will directly test PET-degrading activity.

3. Hit 3 significance:
E = 0.082 is NOT significant — it means approximately 0.08 random matches of this quality would be expected by chance in this database search. Convention (E < 0.001) is not met, and even if a threshold were set higher, the 18% identity over 45% coverage provides no reliable information about shared function. Additionally, the annotation “TPA: reassembled from uncultured metagenome, computationally predicted” means there is no experimental evidence for this protein’s existence or function — any functional annotation is entirely derived from computational similarity to other entries, making it circular if used to infer your protein’s function. This hit should be discarded.

4. AlphaFold2 plDDT interpretation:
plDDT (predicted local distance difference test) > 90: very high confidence — the α/β hydrolase fold domain structure is likely accurate and suitable for functional analysis, active site identification, and structural comparisons. plDDT 32–45 for the C-terminal 40-residue region: very low confidence — this region is predicted with low reliability. Possible interpretations: (i) the region is intrinsically disordered (lacks stable 3D structure in solution) — common for terminal extensions and linker regions; (ii) insufficient evolutionary information in the MSA to constrain the structure prediction; (iii) the region adopts different conformations in different contexts. Low-confidence regions should NOT be used for functional inference (e.g. do not attempt to identify binding sites or predict interactions from this region). They should be experimentally characterised — NMR (suitable for disordered regions), cryo-EM, or deletion constructs to assess whether the C-terminal region is essential for activity, stability, or protein-protein interactions.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: During the COVID-19 pandemic, phylogenetic analysis of SARS-CoV-2 genomes was used to trace transmission chains, identify variants of concern, and investigate the virus’s origins. The most contentious phylogenetic question was whether SARS-CoV-2 originated from a natural zoonotic spillover from bats (via an intermediate host) or from a laboratory incident (lab leak). Evaluate: (a) what phylogenetic methods can and cannot demonstrate about viral origins; (b) what non-phylogenetic evidence bears on the origin question; (c) why this question proved scientifically difficult to resolve despite enormous global attention; and (d) what this case illustrates about the relationship between scientific evidence and public discourse on contested questions.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) What phylogenetics can and cannot demonstrate:
Phylogenetics established clearly that SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the sarbecovirus lineage of betacoronaviruses and is most closely related to RaTG13 (bat coronavirus, ~96.1% genome identity, collected in Yunnan province, China) and BANAL-52/103 (bat coronaviruses from Laos, even closer in the receptor-binding domain). This conclusively rules out SARS-CoV-1 or MERS-CoV as progenitors and identifies bats as the most likely ultimate reservoir. Phylogenetics cannot distinguish between natural spillover (virus jumped to humans directly or via intermediate host) and lab leak (virus was being studied in a laboratory and escaped). Both scenarios would produce the same phylogenetic signal — a virus closely related to bat coronaviruses. Phylogenetics traces ancestry; it does not record the environment in which the virus last resided before human transmission. The absence of a clear intermediate host sequence does not favour lab leak — the progenitor of SARS-CoV-1 was not identified for years after the epidemic, and most bat habitats remain unsampled.

(b) Non-phylogenetic evidence:
Epidemiological evidence: early cases clustered geographically near the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market in Wuhan, and environmental sampling found SARS-CoV-2 RNA specifically in the market’s wildlife stalls — consistent with, though not proving, zoonotic spillover at the market. Molecular features: the SARS-CoV-2 furin cleavage site (PRRA insert at the S1/S2 boundary) was cited by lab-leak proponents as unusual — but similar features have since been found in natural bat sarbecovirus sequences, reducing its significance as a unique engineered marker. Laboratory evidence: the Wuhan Institute of Virology conducted coronavirus research under biosafety level 2 and 3 conditions; a US intelligence community assessment (low confidence) suggested a lab-related incident; the WIV’s virus database was taken offline in September 2019. However, no public evidence of SARS-CoV-2 or a direct progenitor being studied at the WIV has been produced. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but the burden of positive evidence for lab origin has not been met publicly.

(c) Why resolution proved difficult:
Several factors compounded: (i) the COVID-19 pandemic itself created political and geopolitical pressures that made transparency difficult — China’s government restricted access to early patient data, wildlife samples, and laboratory records; (ii) the question requires evidence from facilities and databases that have not been fully shared; (iii) distinguishing natural virus features from engineered ones is genuinely hard when natural sarbecoviruses remain incompletely characterised; (iv) the intermediate host has not been identified, which is scientifically inconclusive but became disproportionately construed as evidence for lab origin. Scientific investigation requires access; access was limited by politics; therefore genuine scientific resolution of this specific question could not be completed with available public evidence.

(d) Science and public discourse on contested questions:
The COVID-19 origins debate illustrates several tensions. First, scientific uncertainty was misrepresented — the absence of a definitive natural spillover proof was presented as evidence for lab leak, when absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence. Second, legitimate scientific questions (lab leak is genuinely possible, even if evidence does not currently favour it) became conflated with politically motivated claims, making dispassionate analysis harder. Third, peer-review systems designed for normal science pace struggled with a rapidly evolving public health emergency — preprints proliferated without peer review, and some were amplified uncritically. Fourth, the social media ecosystem amplified high-confidence minority views over cautious mainstream ones. The epistemologically appropriate position — “available evidence moderately favours natural spillover but is insufficient to exclude lab origin, and we cannot resolve this without further access to data” — was difficult to communicate and politically unsatisfying to all parties. Science communication must become better at articulating probabilistic, uncertain conclusions without being misrepresented as evasive or uncommitted.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Sequencing of DNA extracted directly from environmental samples (soil, seawater, gut contents) without prior cultivation — revealing the genetic diversity of entire microbial communities. The human gut microbiome, ocean virome, and soil resistome have all been characterised by metagenomic approaches.

Large language models trained on protein sequences (analogous to LLMs trained on text) that learn statistical patterns of amino acid co-occurrence, enabling structure and function prediction without explicit evolutionary information. ESM-2 and related models achieve near-AlphaFold accuracy using transformer architectures.

Orthologous genes share a common ancestor via speciation (e.g. human insulin and mouse insulin); paralogous genes share a common ancestor via gene duplication within a genome (e.g. human haemoglobin α and β chains). Orthologues usually share function; paralogues may have diverged in function — an important distinction when inferring function from homology.

A bioinformatics workflow for identifying SNPs associated with traits or diseases: quality control of genotyping arrays, imputation using reference panels (1000 Genomes, HRC), population stratification correction (PCA of ancestry), association testing, and fine-mapping — producing Manhattan plots and Q-Q plots for result visualisation.

Analysis of genomic sequences across multiple species to identify conserved functional elements (genes under purifying selection) and rapidly evolving regions (adaptive evolution) — exploiting the principle that biologically important sequences are conserved across evolutionary time. Used to predict regulatory elements, identify candidate disease genes, and reconstruct ancestral genomes.

The bioinformatics process of identifying positions in a sequenced genome that differ from the reference sequence, from raw sequencing reads — requiring alignment, deduplication, base quality score recalibration, and variant calling (GATK HaplotypeCaller or Mutect2 for somatic variants). False positives and false negatives are endemic at low sequencing coverage.

questions.questionHtml: A BLAST search returns a hit with E-value = 10⁻⁴⁵. Which statement correctly interprets this E-value?
options: Approximately 10⁻⁴⁵ random alignments of this quality or better would be expected by chance in a database of this size — the hit is almost certainly a genuine homologue
There is a 10⁻⁴⁵ probability that this alignment is correct — meaning the alignment is very uncertain
The two sequences share 45% identity — a borderline case requiring further analysis
The E-value confirms that the two proteins have the same biological function
questions.correctAnswer: Approximately 10⁻⁴⁵ random alignments of this quality or better would be expected by chance in a database of this size — the hit is almost certainly a genuine homologue
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The E-value (expect value) is the number of random hits of this quality expected by chance. At 10⁻⁴⁵, this is essentially zero — far below even the most stringent significance thresholds. The alignment is almost certainly non-random and reflects genuine evolutionary relationship.

questions.questionHtml: In an RNA-seq experiment comparing gene expression in cancer cells vs normal cells, testing 20,000 genes at p<0.05 threshold without multiple testing correction would be expected to produce approximately how many false positive ‘differentially expressed’ genes?
options: ~5 false positives — the p-value of 0.05 means there is only a 5% chance of any single false positive across all tests
Zero — p-values control the false positive rate globally across all tests simultaneously
~200 false positives — RNA-seq data is correlated between genes, reducing independent tests from 20,000 to ~4,000
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. At a per-test type I error rate of α = 0.05, testing 20,000 genes independently would produce ~1,000 false positives (20,000 × 0.05 = 1,000) even if no genes were genuinely differentially expressed. Multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, Bonferroni) adjusts the threshold to control the false discovery rate across all tests simultaneously.

questions.questionHtml: A research team publishes an AlphaFold2 structure of a novel membrane protein with plDDT of 88 for transmembrane helices and 38 for an extracellular loop. They claim the extracellular loop structure reveals a specific drug binding site and propose designing inhibitors to target it. Critically evaluate this claim.
options: The claim is unwarranted for the extracellular loop — plDDT of 38 indicates very low confidence in that region’s predicted structure, likely reflecting intrinsic disorder or insufficient evolutionary constraints, making it unsuitable for drug design without experimental structural validation
The claim is valid because AlphaFold2 predictions are now considered equivalent to experimentally determined structures for all protein regions
The claim is invalid because AlphaFold2 cannot predict membrane protein structures — it is only validated for soluble proteins
The claim is reasonable because extracellular loops are inherently disordered and all drug design targeting loops accepts high uncertainty
questions.correctAnswer: The claim is unwarranted for the extracellular loop — plDDT of 38 indicates very low confidence in that region’s predicted structure, likely reflecting intrinsic disorder or insufficient evolutionary constraints, making it unsuitable for drug design without experimental structural validation
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. plDDT < 50 is considered very low confidence — the predicted coordinates for the extracellular loop are unreliable. AlphaFold2 itself cautions that low-confidence regions should not be used for structural inference. Drug design based on an inaccurate binding site model would produce invalid pharmacophore hypotheses. The transmembrane helices (plDDT 88) could reasonably be used for structural analysis, but the extracellular loop requires experimental validation (cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography, or NMR) before drug design is warranted.
